lesson.child_mission: Sides meet at corners (vertices). An angle is the turn between two sides. A right angle is a square corner; other angles can be smaller or larger than a right angle.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same method to a larger number or a new context, then compare two solution paths for accuracy.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
How many right angles in a rectangle? Mark angles in a right-angled triangle as right / smaller / larger than right.

FEEDBACK
4 right angles; one right, two acute (smaller than right) typically.

WATCH FOR
Calling every sharp-looking corner a right angle without testing is inaccurate.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
On twelve shapes, count sides and corners, then label each angle as right, smaller than right, or larger than right using a paper corner tester.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Calling every sharp-looking corner a right angle without testing is inaccurate. Correction: 4 right angles; one right, two acute (smaller than right) typically.

Parent: Likely misconception: Calling every sharp-looking corner a right angle without testing is inaccurate. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Sides meet at corners (vertices). An angle is the turn between two sides. A right angle is a square corner; other angles can be smaller or larger than a right angle.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.
